guide.title: Pigna, Rome: the Pantheon, the Largo Argentina temples and the Jesuit quarter
guide.intro: Pigna is the ninth of Rome's twenty-two rioni, and it is small and very densely built. The Pantheon stands in it. So do two Jesuit churches, the Gesu and Sant'Ignazio di Loyola; the Dominican basilica of Santa Maria sopra Minerva; four Republican temples in the sunken archaeological enclosure at Largo di Torre Argentina; a fifteenth-century palace that is now a national museum and a national research library; a family palace with its own picture gallery on via del Corso; and the sixteenth-century Jesuit college that today houses the Ministero della Cultura. Almost every edge of the rione is a street or a square shared with one of five neighbours. Via della Pigna and piazza della Pigna carry the rione's name.

sections.heading: Pigna's edges
sections.body:
Pigna's edges are streets and squares it shares with five neighbouring rioni. it.wikipedia's article on the rione gives them as via del Seminario, piazza Sant'Ignazio and via del Caravita with Colonna; via del Corso, piazza San Marcello and piazza Venezia with Trevi; via San Marco with Campitelli; via delle Botteghe Oscure and via Florida with Sant'Angelo; and via della Torre Argentina, piazza Santa Chiara, via della Rotonda and piazza della Rotonda with Sant'Eustachio. A street named as a boundary is evidence of a line, not of what stands on either side of it.

Start with piazza della Rotonda, the square the Pantheon faces. OpenStreetMap's rione boundary data puts most of that square in Colonna, while it.wikipedia, citing Roma Capitale's own street register, describes it as a junction of three rioni and names a third party, Sant'Eustachio, that the geometry does not return at all. The two readings do not reconcile, and no source settles the rione of the square, of the fountain standing in it, or of the obelisk on that fountain. The Pantheon itself is in Pigna. The sources are divided over piazza Venezia in the same way. Palazzo Venezia, the basilica of San Marco and the museum and library inside the palazzo complex are a different matter: each stands in Pigna.

Two more boundaries are worth knowing before you walk. The church of Sant'Ignazio di Loyola is in Pigna; the square in front of it is a separate object. And at Largo di Torre Argentina the fenced archaeological area and the open square around it are two different objects with two different answers: the Area Sacra itself is wholly Pigna, while the square is shared with Sant'Eustachio, which also holds the Teatro Argentina.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source establishes a metro station or a bus route for Pigna, and no walking times or distances are given. Steer by addresses instead.

The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the entrance to the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina as via di San Nicola de' Cesarini, opposite no. 10, with the ticket office and bookshop in the Torre del Papito on piazza dei Calcarari. The Doria Pamphilj administration gives the gallery entrance as Via del Corso 305, 00186 Roma. VIVE, the state institute that runs Palazzo Venezia, is addressed at Piazza Venezia 1 for the Museo Nazionale del Palazzo di Venezia and Piazza Venezia 3 for the Biblioteca di Archeologia e Storia dell'Arte. Roma Capitale gives Piazza della Minerva 42 for Santa Maria sopra Minerva. The Pontificia Accademia Ecclesiastica is at Piazza della Minerva 74, in Palazzo Severoli.

One trap is worth naming, because it defeats map software as well as visitors. Several Pigna buildings, Palazzo Doria Pamphilj and Palazzo De Carolis among them, carry via del Corso addresses, but the carriageway of the Corso is itself a rione boundary. A street address is not a claim about which rione a building stands in. The streets that lie wholly inside Pigna, and that this guide uses for orientation rather than as records, are via del Plebiscito, via dei Cestari, via del Gesu, via del Pie di Marmo, via della Gatta and via di Torre Argentina.

sections.heading: Tickets and opening hours
sections.body:
The Pantheon's own site gives daily opening of 09.00 to 19.00, last entry 18.30, closed on 1 January and 25 December, and states that entry has been paid since 3 July 2023 and is free on the first Sunday of the month. No admission price is stated.

For the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina the Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives Tuesday to Sunday, 10.00 to 16.00 in winter and 10.00 to 19.00 in summer, with 9.30 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December, closed Mondays, 25 December and 1 May, with entry timed every twenty minutes. Its published tariff is 7.00 euro full and 4.00 euro reduced for non-residents, plus 1.00 euro advance booking; entry is free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence, and free on the first Sunday of the month subject to capacity. Read those two figures as the non-resident price, because that is what they are.

The Galleria Doria Pamphilj gives Monday to Thursday 09.00 to 19.00, last entry 18.00, and Friday to Sunday 10.00 to 20.00, last entry 19.00, closed every Wednesday and on 1 January, Easter and 25 December, with booking advised and no cloakroom. Its site is explicit that the Appartamenti Segreti with the Bagno di Diana are run separately and are not included in the gallery ticket. Roma Capitale gives Sant'Ignazio di Loyola as open Monday to Sunday 09.00 to 23.30, with masses Monday to Saturday at 18.30 and Sunday at 11.30 and 18.30, and gives Santa Maria sopra Minerva mass times of 18.00 Monday to Saturday and 11.00 and 18.00 on Sundays and feast days. For the Chiesa del Gesu, Roma Capitale carries separate winter and summer schedules, so check its page against the season you are travelling in.

Two things inside the rione are not simply walk-in. VIVE's site carries a standing notice that the Sale Storiche of Palazzo Venezia are closed to the public for restoration, with 2026 given as the notice's horizon. And the Sala della Crociera in the Collegio Romano is normally open only to scholars; VIVE opened it to the public through the programme Incontriamoci al Collegio Romano, four lecture cycles and special openings running from March to December 2026.

faq.question: Is the Pantheon in Pigna?
faq.answer: Yes. The Pantheon is in Pigna. The square it faces is a different question: OpenStreetMap puts most of piazza della Rotonda in Colonna, while it.wikipedia, citing Roma Capitale's street register, calls the square a junction of three rioni. Because those readings do not agree, this guide states no rione for the square, for the fountain in it, or for the obelisk on that fountain, and writes only the building.

faq.question: What is the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina, and can you go in?
faq.answer: It is a sunken archaeological enclosure holding four Republican temples, known as A, B, C and D, together with the remains of the church of San Nicola de Calcarario and the medieval Torre del Papito. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that demolition of the old quarter began in 1926 and that the site was inaugurated on 21 April 1929 by Benito Mussolini; it reopened to the public on 20 June 2023 with a walkway funded by Bulgari. Entry is from via di San Nicola de' Cesarini, opposite no. 10, and the ticket office and bookshop are in the Torre del Papito on piazza dei Calcarari.

faq.question: Was Julius Caesar killed here?
faq.answer: The ruined hall at the west of the Area Sacra is identified as the Curia of Pompey. it.wikipedia records the tradition that Julius Caesar was killed there in 44 BC. Roma Capitale's own account of the Area Sacra does not mention it, which is why this guide reports the tradition and its source rather than stating it as fact.

faq.question: Is Palazzo Maffei Marescotti part of the Vatican?
faq.answer: No. The palazzo stands in Pigna, on the corner of via dei Cestari and via della Pigna, on Italian soil. The Holy See's own published list of its extraterritorial properties in Rome includes it. Extraterritoriality is the immunity international law grants to the headquarters of a foreign state's diplomatic agents; it is not part of Vatican City, it is not Vatican territory, it is not a border, and a visitor there is under Italian law. Two other Holy See bodies in the rione, the Pontificia Accademia Ecclesiastica on piazza della Minerva and the Pontificio Seminario Francese, are not on that list at all.

faq.question: Which of Pigna's churches can be visited most easily?
faq.answer: Three carry published hours or mass times. Roma Capitale gives Sant'Ignazio di Loyola as open Monday to Sunday from 09.00 to 23.30, with masses Monday to Saturday at 18.30 and Sunday at 11.30 and 18.30. It gives Santa Maria sopra Minerva mass times of 18.00 Monday to Saturday and 11.00 and 18.00 on Sundays and feast days. For the Chiesa del Gesu it carries winter and summer schedules that differ, so check its page for the season. The Camere di Sant'Ignazio, the rooms where Ignatius of Loyola lived and died, are in the Casa professa on the same square as the Gesu.

faq.question: Is anything in Pigna free to enter?
faq.answer: The Pantheon's own site states that entry, paid since 3 July 2023, is free on the first Sunday of the month. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina is free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence, and free on the first Sunday of the month subject to capacity. Beyond ticketed sites, the fountains and street sculpture of the rione cost nothing: the Fontana della Pigna and the talking statue Madama Lucrezia on piazza San Marco, the Fontana del Facchino on via Lata, the marble foot on via del Pie di Marmo and the elephant and obelisk on piazza della Minerva.

photos.title: The elephant and obelisk on piazza della Minerva
photos.description: The marble elephant carrying the Minerveo obelisk on piazza della Minerva, carved by Ercole Ferrata to a 1667 design by Gian Lorenzo Bernini and known in Rome as the Pulcin della Minerva, standing in front of the facade of the basilica of Santa Maria sopra Minerva.
photos.author: Livioandronico2013

places.name: Pantheon
places.summary: The Roman temple that is now the basilica of Santa Maria ad Martyres. It stands in Pigna, although the square it faces does not. Its own site gives daily opening of 09.00 to 19.00, last entry 18.30, closed on 1 January and 25 December. Entry has been paid since 3 July 2023 and is free on the first Sunday of the month.
places.history: The Pantheon's own account says that Agrippa built the temple in 27 BC and dedicated it to the seven planetary divinities, from which the name Pantheon, of all the gods; that the original building was smaller; and that Hadrian rebuilt it between 118 and 125 AD. The same account records that Raphael chose the Pantheon as his burial place.

places.name: Area Sacra di Largo Argentina
places.address: Via di San Nicola de' Cesarini, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A sunken archaeological enclosure in the middle of the city holding four Republican temples, the remains of the church of San Nicola de Calcarario and the medieval Torre del Papito. Entry is on via di San Nicola de' Cesarini, opposite no. 10; the ticket office and bookshop are in the Torre del Papito, piazza dei Calcarari. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday, 10.00 to 16.00 in winter and 10.00 to 19.00 in summer, with 9.30 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December, closed Mondays, 25 December and 1 May. Its published tariff is 7.00 euro full and 4.00 euro reduced for non-residents, plus 1.00 euro advance booking; entry is free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence, and free on the first Sunday of the month subject to capacity. Entry is timed every twenty minutes.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that demolition of the old quarter here began in 1926 and that the site was inaugurated on 21 April 1929 by Benito Mussolini. It reopened to the public on 20 June 2023 with a walkway, funded by Bulgari. A cat colony, the Colonia felina di Torre Argentina, lives in the Area Sacra. The fourth temple platform, Tempio D, lies within the same enclosure and is treated here as part of it rather than as a separate site.

places.name: Tempio A, Area Sacra di Largo Argentina
places.summary: One of the four Republican temples in the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina, and the one a medieval church was later built inside. It is sometimes labelled Tempio delle Ninfe, but that name comes from OpenStreetMap's tagging and is not the name the Sovrintendenza Capitolina uses.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina dates Tempio A to the middle of the third century BC and connects it with the cult of Giuturna.

places.name: Tempio B, Area Sacra di Largo Argentina
places.summary: The round temple among the four in the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina dates Tempio B to the late second century BC and connects it with Fortuna huiusce diei.

places.name: Tempio C, Area Sacra di Largo Argentina
places.summary: One of the four Republican temples in the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places the building of Tempio C at the start of the third century BC and says the cult was probably that of Feronia.

places.name: Curia di Pompeo
places.summary: The ruined hall at the west of the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina is identified as the Curia of Pompey.
places.history: it.wikipedia records the tradition that Julius Caesar was killed there in 44 BC; Roma Capitale's own account of the Area Sacra does not mention it. This record reports the tradition and its source rather than asserting it.

places.name: Torre del Papito
places.summary: The medieval tower on the edge of the Area Sacra, and the practical heart of a visit: the Sovrintendenza Capitolina puts the archaeological site's ticket office and bookshop inside it, and uses its portico as one of the two display areas.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina is careful about the tower's origins, saying that the fragmentary notices attribute it to the Papareschi and placing it in the fourteenth century. It records the popular derivation of the name from the antipope Anacleto II, called the Papetto, and traces the tower through the Foschi de Judeis, the Boccamazza and the Cesarini, and its appearance on the Nolli plan.

places.name: Chiesa di San Nicola de Calcarario
places.summary: The remains of a church built inside the shell of Tempio A, visible within the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina, and a direct illustration of how medieval Rome reused a Republican temple rather than clearing it away.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records the first evidence of a church inside temple A in the ninth century, its dedication to St Nicholas in 1132, and its names, first de' Calcarario and then de' Cesarini. Part of the decorated twelfth-century apse survives. The Baroque church that stood above it was destroyed in the Governatorato demolitions.

places.name: Terme di Agrippa
places.address: Via dell'Arco della Ciambella, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: Via dell'Arco della Ciambella takes its name from a surviving arched fragment of the Baths of Agrippa. This is a street-side remnant, not a site to go into, and no visiting arrangements are published for it.
places.history: The identification of the fragment with the Baths of Agrippa is recorded by it.wikipedia; no institutional source was obtained for it.

places.name: Pie di Marmo
places.address: Via del Pie di Marmo, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A colossal marble foot standing at street level, and the reason the street around it is called via del Pie di Marmo.
places.history: The fragment is popularly associated with the Temple of Isis that stood in this quarter. That association is popular tradition rather than an institutional attribution.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria sopra Minerva
places.summary: The basilica stands on piazza della Minerva. Roma Capitale gives the address as Piazza della Minerva 42 and mass times of 18.00 Monday to Saturday and 11.00 and 18.00 on Sundays and feast days.
places.history: It holds the remains of Catherine of Siena, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and of Fra Angelico, proclaimed universal patron of artists in 1984, and a fresco by Melozzo da Forli.

places.name: Chiesa del Gesu
places.summary: The mother church of the Society of Jesus, on the square that carries its name. Roma Capitale's tourism page carries separate winter and summer opening and mass schedules for it, so check that page against the season you are travelling in.
places.history: The church's own history says that Ignatius commissioned a design from Nanni di Baccio Biggio in 1551; that Michelangelo redrew the plan in 1554, unbuilt; that Cardinal Alessandro Farnese funded the work in 1561 and gave it to Vignola; that construction began in 1568; and that Giacomo della Porta designed the facade and completed the work in 1575, the church being dedicated in 1584. The painted decoration by Baciccia and the transept chapels of St Francis Xavier and St Ignatius belong to the later seventeenth century.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Ignazio di Loyola
places.summary: The other Jesuit church in this rione, and the one with Andrea Pozzo's painted ceiling. Roma Capitale gives opening Monday to Sunday 09.00 to 23.30, masses Monday to Saturday at 18.30 and Sunday at 11.30 and 18.30. The church's own site describes it as being in the quartiere Campo Marzio: that is the ancient Campus Martius, not the rione of the same name, and the church stands in Pigna. The square in front of it is a separate object and is not written as a Pigna place.
places.history: The church's own account records that Gregory XV gave the commission to Orazio Grassi and that the church was consecrated in 1722. Andrea Pozzo, a Jesuit and a painter, made the interior decorations in 1685: the false dome, the vault and the presbytery. Aloysius Gonzaga, John Berchmans and Robert Bellarmine are buried here.

places.name: Basilica di San Marco Evangelista al Campidoglio
places.summary: A basilica standing against the flank of Palazzo Venezia, on piazza San Marco. It stands in Pigna; the Campidoglio in its name is a dedication and not a statement about which rione it is in. The travertine pine-cone fountain and the talking statue Madama Lucrezia both stand outside it.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the basilica was founded in 336 by Pope Mark, appears as Titulus Marci in the synod acts of 499, and gained its Renaissance benediction loggia under Paul II in 1465 to 1470.

places.name: Camere di Sant'Ignazio
places.summary: The rooms in which Ignatius of Loyola lived and died, in the Casa professa on the same square as the Chiesa del Gesu.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page for the Gesu states that the Casa professa on the square houses the Camere di Sant'Ignazio, where the saint lived and died, and that they retain their original decoration by Andrea Pozzo and Borgognone.

places.name: Palazzo Venezia
places.summary: VIVE, the state institute that runs the palazzo, describes it as a fifteenth-century residence of popes, cardinals and ambassadors, its facades and much of its detail going back to its founder and first occupant Cardinal Pietro Barbo, who became Paul II from 1464 to 1471. Paul III Farnese, from 1534 to 1549, was among later papal residents, and Erasmus and Charles V among recorded guests. VIVE's site carries a standing notice that the Sale Storiche are closed to the public for restoration; the notice gives 2026 as its horizon, so check before travelling.
places.history: The palazzo stands in the rione Pigna, and it.wikipedia places it in Pigna in the opening sentence of its article. The square it fronts, piazza Venezia, is a different matter: the sources disagree about which rione that square belongs to, and this guide states no rione for it.

places.name: Museo Nazionale del Palazzo di Venezia
places.summary: The national museum inside Palazzo Venezia, addressed at Piazza Venezia 1. It is part of VIVE, an istituto autonomo of the Ministero della Cultura. No opening hours or admission prices are published here, because none were obtained; VIVE's standing notice about the closure of the palazzo's Sale Storiche for restoration applies to any visit.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the museum.

places.name: Biblioteca di Archeologia e Storia dell'Arte (BiASA)
places.summary: VIVE describes the BiASA as a public research library of the Ministero della Cultura specialising in archaeology, architecture and art history, founded in 1875 out of the book collection of the Direzione Generale Antichita e Belle Arti, and holding the archaeologist Rodolfo Lanciani's collection on deposit. Its Palazzo Venezia reading room reopened to the public on 28 April 2025 after consolidation and restoration work.
places.history: The library keeps a detached section elsewhere in this rione: the Sala della Crociera in the Collegio Romano has belonged to the BiASA since 1989.

places.name: Palazzo Doria Pamphilj
places.summary: A family palace occupying most of a block between via del Corso and the streets behind it, still in family administration and open as a house museum through its picture gallery. Its address is on the Corso, but it stands in Pigna.
places.history: The family administration's own account describes a palace built on the core of Cardinal Fazio Santoro's early sixteenth-century residence and grown by annexation over five hundred years, through the Della Rovere, Aldobrandini, Pamphilj, Doria Pamphilj, Facchinetti, Colonna, Borghese and Savoia families. The gallery took its present form between 1731 and 1734, when Prince Camillo Pamphilj the younger commissioned Gabriele Valvassori to rework the Corso range.

places.name: Galleria Doria Pamphilj
places.summary: The picture gallery inside Palazzo Doria Pamphilj, entered from Via del Corso 305. Its own site gives Monday to Thursday 09.00 to 19.00 with last entry at 18.00, and Friday to Sunday 10.00 to 20.00 with last entry at 19.00; it is closed every Wednesday and on 1 January, Easter and 25 December. There is no cloakroom and booking is advised.
places.history: The pictures still hang to the late eighteenth-century arrangement documented in a 1767 manuscript held in the family archive. One caveat is worth knowing before booking: the Appartamenti Segreti with the Bagno di Diana are run separately, and the site states they are not included in the gallery ticket.

places.name: Collegio Romano
places.address: Piazza del Collegio Romano, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The Jesuit college building on piazza del Collegio Romano. VIVE describes it as the current seat of the Ministero della Cultura. Most of it is working offices rather than a visitor site; the part that opens to the public is the Sala della Crociera on its second floor.
places.history: VIVE describes the Collegio Romano as the majestic palace built between 1581 and 1584 at the wish of Pope Gregory XIII Boncompagni as the seat of the Studio della Compagnia di Gesu. Where it.wikipedia gives 1582 for the start of building, this guide follows VIVE.

places.name: Sala della Crociera
places.address: Piazza del Collegio Romano, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The historic library hall on the second floor of the Collegio Romano. VIVE states that it is normally open only to scholars, and that it was opened to the public through the programme Incontriamoci al Collegio Romano, four lecture cycles and special openings running from March to December 2026. Anyone reading this after that programme has ended should assume scholarly access only until VIVE says otherwise.
places.history: The hall housed the Bibliotheca Maior of the Jesuit Studio. Since 1989 it has been a detached section of the Biblioteca di Archeologia e Storia dell'Arte, whose main reading room is in Palazzo Venezia.

places.name: Palazzo De Carolis
places.summary: An eighteenth-century palace on via del Corso, and one of the Pigna buildings whose Corso address misleads: the carriageway of the Corso is a rione boundary, while the palace itself stands in Pigna.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that after the demolition in 1724 of the painter Jacopino del Conte's house, the wall fountain known as the Fontana del Facchino was reset on the main front of Palazzo De Carolis-Simonetti, and that in 1872 to 1873 it was moved again, to via Lata, for reasons of traffic.

places.name: Palazzo Maffei Marescotti
places.summary: Palazzo Maffei Marescotti stands on the corner of via dei Cestari and via della Pigna, adjoining the church of the Santissime Stimmate di San Francesco. The Holy See's own published list of its extraterritorial properties in Rome includes il Palazzo Maffei o del Vicariato, noting that it was formerly the seat of the diocesan Curia of Rome and that the Curia still has some offices there. Extraterritoriality is the immunity international law grants to the headquarters of a foreign state's diplomatic agents. The building stands on Italian soil, it is not part of Vatican City, it is not a border, and a visitor there is under Italian law.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Giacomo della Porta designed the palazzo in 1580 for Cardinal Marcantonio Maffei, who died in 1583 leaving it unfinished; that it passed through Camilla Peretti, a Sannesio, Cardinal Ludovisi in 1621, Francesco II d'Este in 1668 and an Acciaiuoli in 1714 to the Marescotti in 1764, who had Ferdinando Fuga enlarge it; and that it was sold to the Banca Romana in 1865 and bought by the Holy See in 1906, which made it the seat of the Vicariate of Rome until the Vicariate moved to the Palazzo di San Callisto in 1964.

places.name: Piazza della Minerva
places.summary: Roma Capitale's tourism service carries piazza della Minerva as a place in its own right. The basilica of Santa Maria sopra Minerva fronts it, the marble elephant carrying an obelisk stands in the middle of it, the Pontificia Accademia Ecclesiastica is at no. 74, and the Grand Hotel de la Minerve occupies a palazzo on the same square.
places.history: No source states a separate institutional history of the square.

places.name: Obelisco della Minerva
places.summary: The obelisk on piazza della Minerva stands on the back of a marble elephant carved by Ercole Ferrata to a 1667 design by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, and is popularly called the Pulcin della Minerva.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the Egyptian obelisk came from the Iseo Campense, the temple of Isis that stood in this quarter. Roma Capitale's tourism service and it.wikipedia give different dates for the obelisk itself, and no source settles it.

places.name: Piazza del Gesu
places.summary: Roma Capitale gives piazza del Gesu as the address of the Chiesa del Gesu, and the Casa professa holding the Camere di Sant'Ignazio fronts the same square.
places.history: No source states a separate institutional history of the square.

places.name: Piazza dei Calcarari
places.summary: The small square on the edge of the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina names it as the address of the archaeological site's ticket office and bookshop, which are inside the Torre del Papito.
places.history: No source states a separate institutional history of the square.

places.name: Fontana della Pigna
places.summary: A travertine pine-cone fountain stands in front of San Marco.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the Comune di Roma erected it, to a design by Pietro Lombardi, to restore the rione's emblem after the ancient bronze pine cone was moved away.

places.name: Fontana del Facchino
places.summary: A wall fountain in the form of a porter holding a barrel, set into a building front on via Lata, and one of the Roman talking statues.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the fountain, anciently called the barrel or half-barrel, was made at the expense and to the design of the Florentine painter Jacopino del Conte to ornament his house on via del Corso, between 1580 and 1598, the year of his death. After the house was demolished in 1724 the fountain was reset on the main front of Palazzo De Carolis-Simonetti, and in 1872 to 1873 it was moved to via Lata for reasons of traffic. The Sovrintendenza counts it among the Congresso degli arguti, with Pasquino, Marforio, the abate Luigi, Madama Lucrezia and the Babuino.

places.name: Madama Lucrezia
places.summary: A marble bust standing to the left of the entrance to the basilica of San Marco, at the Palazzo di San Marco, and one of the Roman talking statues.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes it as possibly a portrait of Faustina, and as coming from the Temple of Isis. It records that the bust has been publicly displayed at the Palazzo di San Marco since the fifteenth century, and counts it among the Congresso degli arguti alongside the Fontana del Facchino.

places.name: Pontificia Accademia Ecclesiastica
places.summary: The Pontificia Accademia Ecclesiastica, the Holy See's diplomatic academy, is at Piazza della Minerva 74, in Palazzo Severoli. It is a working institution rather than a visitor site, and no public access is published for it.
places.history: It does not appear on the Holy See's published list of its extraterritorial properties in Rome, and nothing in this guide should be read as suggesting that it enjoys that status.

places.name: Ditta Annibale Gammarelli
places.summary: Ditta Annibale Gammarelli, on via Santa Chiara, sells sacred vestments, episcopal insignia and ecclesiastical tailoring; its strapline is Nobilitas in Traditione.
places.history: The shop belongs to the cluster of ecclesiastical outfitters around via dei Cestari and via di Santa Caterina da Siena. No dates and no claims about how long it has traded are published here, because the business makes none on its own site.

places.name: Ditta G. Poggi
places.summary: An artists' materials shop in the rione. The business calls itself Ditta G. Poggi - Belle Arti dal 1825; that is its name, and this guide prints it as a name rather than as a statement of how long the shop has traded.
places.history: No source states a history of the business.

places.name: Grand Hotel de la Minerve
places.summary: The Grand Hotel de la Minerve occupies a palazzo on piazza della Minerva.
places.history: No source states a history, rating or description of the hotel.

entries.name: Pantheon
entries.note: Agrippa's temple of 27 BC, rebuilt by Hadrian between 118 and 125 AD, now the basilica of Santa Maria ad Martyres and the burial place Raphael chose.

entries.name: Area Sacra di Largo Argentina
entries.note: Four Republican temples in a sunken enclosure, reopened to the public on 20 June 2023 with a walkway; entry is timed every twenty minutes and closed on Mondays.

entries.name: Curia di Pompeo
entries.note: The ruined hall at the west of the enclosure, where it.wikipedia records the tradition that Julius Caesar was killed in 44 BC.

entries.name: Torre del Papito
entries.note: The fourteenth-century tower on piazza dei Calcarari holds the archaeological site's ticket office and bookshop, and its portico serves as a display area.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria sopra Minerva
entries.note: It holds the remains of Catherine of Siena and of Fra Angelico, and a fresco by Melozzo da Forli; mass is at 18.00 Monday to Saturday.

entries.name: Obelisco della Minerva
entries.note: An Egyptian obelisk from the Iseo Campense, riding a marble elephant that Ercole Ferrata carved to a 1667 design by Gian Lorenzo Bernini.

entries.name: Chiesa del Gesu
entries.note: Begun 1568 to Vignola's plan and finished by Giacomo della Porta, who designed the facade, in 1575; dedicated 1584, with Baciccia's painted decoration added later.

entries.name: Camere di Sant'Ignazio
entries.note: The rooms in the Casa professa where Ignatius of Loyola lived and died, keeping their decoration by Andrea Pozzo and Borgognone.

entries.name: Chiesa di Sant'Ignazio di Loyola
entries.note: Andrea Pozzo painted the false dome, the vault and the presbytery in 1685; the church was consecrated in 1722 and opens daily from 09.00 to 23.30.

entries.name: Galleria Doria Pamphilj
entries.note: The pictures still hang to the late eighteenth-century arrangement recorded in a 1767 manuscript; closed every Wednesday, and the Appartamenti Segreti are ticketed separately.

entries.name: Palazzo Venezia
entries.note: A fifteenth-century residence of popes, cardinals and ambassadors, begun by Cardinal Pietro Barbo, who became Paul II in 1464; VIVE gives its Sale Storiche as closed for restoration into 2026.

entries.name: Basilica di San Marco Evangelista al Campidoglio
entries.note: Founded in 336 by Pope Mark and recorded as Titulus Marci in the synod acts of 499, with a benediction loggia added under Paul II in 1465 to 1470.

entries.name: Fontana del Facchino
entries.note: A wall fountain of a porter with a barrel, made for Jacopino del Conte's house between 1580 and 1598 and moved to via Lata in 1872 to 1873 for reasons of traffic.

entries.name: Ditta Annibale Gammarelli
entries.note: Sacred vestments and episcopal insignia, one of the ecclesiastical outfitters clustered around via dei Cestari and via di Santa Caterina da Siena.
